title: Pancreatic Cancer
subject: Pathology
summary: Pancreatic cancer presents with vague abdominal pain, weight loss and jaundice. Diagnosis relies on imaging and tumour markers, while staging guides treatment. Early recognition is vital in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour arising from pancreatic ductal epithelium. It is the most common pancreatic cancer and carries the worst prognosis.
b: Second most common GI cancer after colorectal

sections.p: The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM system is used. Stage I–IV reflects tumour size, nodal status and distant metastasis.

sections.p: Risk factors cluster around chronic inflammation, genetics and environmental exposures. In East Africa, infections and herbal remedies may modify risk.

sections.p: Symptoms are nonspecific and often late. The classic triad is abdominal pain, weight loss and jaundice, but many patients present with only one feature.

t.b: Look for palpable mass, ascites, or jaundice; assess for Trousseau sign (migratory thrombophlebitis).

faq.q: Why is CA 19‑9 not a definitive test?
faq.a: It is sensitive but not specific; many benign conditions raise it, and some tumours do not express it.

faq.q: What is the most common site of metastasis?
faq.a: Liver, followed by peritoneum and lungs.
Only if detected early and resected; most cases are advanced at presentation.

exam: A 58‑year‑old smoker presents with painless jaundice. What is the first investigation? — Abdominal ultrasound to assess biliary obstruction and look for a mass.
A patient with a pancreatic head tumour has a CA 19‑9 of 200 U/mL. What does this suggest? — Elevated marker supports malignancy but is not diagnostic; imaging is required.
During a CT scan, a tumour abuts the superior mesenteric artery. What is the likely management? — The tumour is likely unresectable; consider chemotherapy.
A patient develops sudden abdominal pain and vomiting after starting gemcitabine. What complication should you suspect? — Pancreatitis; monitor enzymes and stop drug if severe.
A 45‑year‑old woman with weight loss has a normal CA 19‑9 but a mass on CT. What is the next step? — Obtain tissue diagnosis via EUS‑FNA.
A patient with pancreatic cancer has a sudden drop in hemoglobin. What is the most likely source? — Upper GI bleeding from tumour ulceration; perform endoscopy.
